questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14082348/assets/94ef52e454545335132d467773c0b274296a7cb3758ae9fae3242876c8063f5f.png)

Find the area $A$ bounded between the curve $x=\frac{3}{4}{y}^{2}-3y$, the $y$-axis, and the lines $y=2$ and $y=4,$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{4}(\frac{3}{4}{y}^{2}-3y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{2}^{4}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,-\,3{\int }_{2}^{4}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot {\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{2}^{4}\,-\,3\cdot {\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}(\frac{64}{3}-\frac{8}{3})\,-\,3(8-2) \\  & =14-18 \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis, we obtained a negative number. So the area that we want is $|-4|=4.$

questions.problem: Find the area bounded between the curve $x=-4{y}^{2}+12,$ the $y$-axis, and the lines $y=0$ and $y=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-4{y}^{2}+12)\,\text{d}y \\  & =-4{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y+12{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-4\cdot {\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1}+12\cdot y{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-4(\frac{1}{3}-0)+12(1-0) \\  & =-\frac{4}{3}+12 \\  & =\frac{32}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area bounded between the curve $x={y}^{2}+2y,$ the $y$-axis, and the lines $y=0$ and $y=-2,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}({y}^{2}+2y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y+2{\int }_{-2}^{0}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{-2}^{0}+2\cdot {\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}|}_{-2}^{0} \\  & =(0-\frac{(-2)^{3}}{3})+2(0-\frac{(-2)^{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}-4 \\  & =-\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis, we obtained a negative number. So the area that we want is $|-\frac{4}{3}|=\frac{4}{3}.$

Find the area $A$ bounded between the curve $x=5{y}^{4}+3$, the $y$-axis, and the lines $y=0$ and $y=1,$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(5{y}^{4}+3)\,\text{d}y \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{4}\,\text{d}y+3{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={y}^{5}\,{|}_{0}^{1}+3y\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =({1}^{5}-{0}^{5})+3(1-0) \\  & =1+3 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the area of the closed region between the curve $x={y}^{3}-6{y}^{2}+9y$ and the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{3}-6{y}^{2}+9y & =0 \\ y({y}^{2}-6y+9) & =0 \\ y(y-3)^{2} & =0 \\ y & =0,3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we draw a sketch of the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14082348/assets/7509bf6a10838458b110d982740c1399aa36279b9ce4a231f99b76d7c7cee0b3.png)

We want to find the area between the curve $x={y}^{3}-6{y}^{2}+9y$ and the $y$-axis from  $y=0$ to $y=3.$ To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}({y}^{3}-6{y}^{2}+9y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y-6{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y+9{\int }_{0}^{3}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{3}-6\cdot {\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{3}+9\cdot {\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =(\frac{{3}^{4}}{4}-0)-6(\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}-0)+9(\frac{{3}^{2}}{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{81}{4}-54+\frac{81}{2} \\  & =\frac{27}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the area of the finite region bounded between the curve $x=9y-{y}^{3}$ and the $y$-axis for $y\ge 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}9y-{y}^{3} & =0 \\ y(9-{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ y & =0,\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we draw a sketch of the region:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14082348/assets/bbcf218e7b6181c861ba4c804357cc53ae6004453914259a9fe98ad5f09ac4d4.png)

We want to find the area between the curve $x=9y-{y}^{3}$ and the $y$-axis from  $y=0$ to $y=3.$ 
To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(9y-{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{3}y\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =9\cdot {\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{3}-{\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =9\cdot (\frac{(3)^{2}}{2}-0)-(\frac{(3)^{4}}{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{81}{2}-\frac{81}{4} \\  & =\frac{81}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}^{3} & =0 \\ y(1-{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ y & =0,\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

From the diagram, we see that we want to find the area between the curve $x=y-{y}^{3}$ and the $y$-axis from $y=0$ to $y=1.$ To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y-{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{1}-{\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{2}-0)-(\frac{1}{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the area between the curve $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2-x)$, the $y$-axis, and the lines $y=-2$ and $y=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make $x$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2-x) \\ {e}^{y} & =2-x \\ x & =2-{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}(2-{e}^{y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{-2}^{0}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{-2}^{0}{e}^{y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\cdot y{|}_{-2}^{0}-{e}^{y}{|}_{-2}^{0} \\  & =2(0+2)-({e}^{0}-{e}^{-2}) \\  & =4-(1-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}) \\  & =3+\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area $A$ between the curve $y=\sqrt[3]{x+8}-2$, the $y$-axis and the lines $y=-2$ and $y=0,$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$

{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make $x$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt[3]{x+8}-2 \\ y+2 & =\sqrt[3]{x+8} \\ (y+2)^{3} & =x+8 \\ x & =(y+2)^{3}-8 \\ x & ={y}^{3}+6{y}^{2}+12y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}({y}^{3}+6{y}^{2}+12y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{-2}^{0}\,+\,6\cdot {\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{-2}^{0}+12\cdot {\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}|}_{-2}^{0} \\  & =(0-\frac{16}{4})+6(0-(-\frac{8}{3}))+12(0-\frac{4}{2}) \\  & =-4+16-24 \\  & =-12\end{aligned}
$$

We obtained a negative number because the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis. So the area that we want is

$$
A=|-12|=12\,.
$$

Find the area $A$ between the curve $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)$, the $y$-axis, and the lines $y=0$ and $y=2.$

$A=$
{{field-1}} .
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make $x$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x) \\ {e}^{y} & =3x \\ x & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{3}{e}^{y}\,dy \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{y}\,dy \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\,{e}^{y}{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({e}^{2}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({e}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

First, we make $x$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt[3]{x-1}+1 \\ y-1 & =\sqrt[3]{x-1} \\ (y-1)^{3} & =x-1 \\ x & =(y-1)^{3}+1 \\ x & ={y}^{3}-3{y}^{2}+3y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{3}-3{y}^{2}+3y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y-3{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y+3{\int }_{0}^{1}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{1}-3\cdot {\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1}+3\cdot {\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{4}-0)-3(\frac{1}{3}-0)+3(\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-1+\frac{3}{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the area of the closed region between the curve $x=y^2-4$ and the $y$-axis.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4 & =0 \\ {y}^{2} & =4 \\ y & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we draw a sketch of the region:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14082348/assets/f2a29faeb9db8e622a21a0e77bea911960a5c64d87a2c900ecd0c0213b2e4bce.png)

We want the area between the curve $x=y^2-4$ and the $y$-axis from  $y=-2$ to $y=2.$ To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}({y}^{2}-4)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}({y}^{2}-4)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-8{\int }_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\cdot {\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{2}-8y{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2(\frac{8}{3}-0)-8(2-0) \\  & =\frac{16}{3}-16 \\  & =-\frac{32}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We obtained a negative number because the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis. So the area that we want is $\left|-\dfrac{32}{3}\right| = \dfrac{32}{3}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{x+1} \\ {y}^{2} & =x+1 \\ x & ={y}^{2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1}-y{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-0)-(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-1 \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We obtained a negative number because the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis. So the area that we want is $\left|-\dfrac{2}{3}\right| = \dfrac{2}{3}.$
